comment.value:
Given the rise of LLM applications in autonomous driving, it is crucial to have datasets and  benchmarks to evaluate the reasoning ability of autonomous driving LLMs in traffic scenes. Existing datasets and benchmarks are mostly focusing on ego-vehicles and monocular videos, whereas in practice, the autonomous driving models have access to multiple views and even multiple types of sensors, such as LiDAR. So having a dataset and benchmark that can assess the autonomous driving LLMs in a multi-modal, multi-view, and multi-frame setting is important. Because the multi-modal multi-view autonomous driving models are usually sensor-setup specific, one dataset and benchmark that works for one model might not be easily translated to work for a different model. Therefore, in addition to having just one dataset and benchmark, having a somewhat automated framework that can generate such a benchmarking dataset from a given well-labeled conventional training dataset is also important.

STSBench was proposed to fill this gap. It not only provides a reasoning benchmarking dataset derived from the NuScenes dataset but also provides a framework that allows the user to prepare reasoning benchmarking dataset from different datasets in a semi-automated fashion. Using the STSBench benchmarking dataset prepared, the paper evaluated reasoning capabilities of representative LLM, general-purpose VLM, and driving expert VLMs and uncovered some critical shortcomings of reasoning in the existing driving expert VLMs.

The major concerns of the paper from the reviewers were:

1. The diversity of the STSBench dataset is somewhat limited.
2. Whether the STSBench framework can be used for preparing reasoning benchmarking dataset from a dataset different from NuScenes.
Some details of the data-mining heuristics and details were not described sufficiently in the paper.

After the rebuttal from the authors, most of the reviewer’s concerns were resolved. This was mainly because:

1. The STSBench dataset limitation mainly comes from the NuScenes dataset limitation. If there is a different dataset that has richer annotations than NuScenes, STSBench framework is competent of mining more diverse and even more edge cases for benchmarking.
2. The authors claim that they are applying the STSBench framework to mine benchmarking dataset from the Argoverse2 dataset to support the claim that the STSBench framework is dataset-agnostic and scalable.
3. The authors have clarified the missing details and will add them into the revised manuscript.

Most of the reviewers considered this paper having a high impact on domains such as autonomous driving. Therefore, I recommend this paper for acceptance.

Thank you for pointing this out, and we apologize for the lack of clarity.

To clarify: in the referenced experiment, we augmented the VLM (InternVL 2.5-8B) with **ground-truth trajectory information in textual form**, identical to what GPT-4o receives, alongside its usual visual input. 
The goal was to evaluate whether combining structured 3D motion data with visual context would enhance the model’s reasoning performance.

Surprisingly, we observed a **slight performance drop**, suggesting that the VLM struggled to effectively **fuse the visual and textual modalities**. 
We hypothesize that the model either failed to align the trajectory descriptions with visual cues, or that the added input increased complexity without meaningful gain, possibly confusing the model.

This result highlights an important limitation: **current VLMs may not yet be equipped to jointly reason over multi-modal inputs that combine structured 3D representations and rich visual context**. 
We will clarify this explanation in the final version of the manuscript.

rebuttal.value:
We thank the reviewer for the thoughtful evaluation and for highlighting key strengths of our work, in particular, the **flexibility of our annotation framework** to construct benchmarks from any perception dataset, the **comprehensive coverage of multi-modal**, **multi-view**, **and multi-frame data**, and the systematic design of scenario questions that offer a well-balanced difficulty distribution and **effectively assess models’ spatio-temporal reasoning capabilities**.


**1. Number of evaluated models**

It is true that the number of evaluated models is limited, particularly in the LLM and VLM categories. These models were included primarily as **baselines** to illustrate the difficulty of the benchmark, despite not being designed or trained for multi-view, spatio-temporal data. Given this mismatch and our resource constraints, we opted not to further expand evaluation in these categories.

In contrast, for **driving expert models**, we conducted a comprehensive evaluation. As shown in **Table 6 of the supplementary material**, we included **all publicly available state-of-the-art models** at the time of submission that offer both executable code and pretrained weights.

We hope our **open-sourced benchmark and codebase** will encourage the community to evaluate additional models in the future, and we welcome such contributions to further strengthen this line of research.


**2. Extreme dangerous scenarios are underrepresented**

We fully agree with the reviewer that the limited presence of dangerous or extreme scenarios in public datasets poses a challenge for evaluating model robustness. This is also acknowledged in the **limitations section** of the main manuscript.

That said, it's important to highlight that even without such edge cases, STSBench already exposes significant weaknesses in current VLMs, particularly in interaction-heavy, multi-agent scenarios. This underscores the benchmark’s utility in evaluating spatio-temporal reasoning under realistic, though not extreme, conditions.

Importantly, our framework is designed to be **easily extendable**. Incorporating rare or hazardous scenarios would only require access to datasets that contain appropriate annotations, along with minor additions to the scenario mining catalog. We see this as a natural and valuable direction for future work, especially as models begin to improve on the current benchmark.


**3. Benchmark mainly based on NuScenes**

We appreciate the reviewer’s concern and clarify that STSBench was designed to be **dataset-agnostic**, even though it is instantiated only on NuScenes in this paper. 

We want to outline this decision based on two significant aspects:


**(1) Instantiation on other datasets:**

We chose to instantiate STSBench solely on NuScenes due to two practical constraints.
First, most existing driving expert VLMs are trained on NuScenes and cannot be directly evaluated on other datasets such as Waymo or Argoverse2, which differ significantly in sensor setups. Second, these alternative datasets currently lack language annotations, making it impossible to train existing driving expert models on them. For this reason, we focused on NuScenes, where both the models and necessary metadata are available.

**(2) Adaptability to different sensor configurations:**

Importantly, our mining framework operates purely on structured annotations, 3D bounding boxes, tracks, class labels, and HD maps, and does not depend on raw sensor data (e.g., images or LiDAR). This makes it **largely independent of sensor configuration**, as long as the dataset provides standard annotations in a common reference frame. Minor adjustments, such as threshold tuning, may be required for different environments (e.g., urban vs. highway), but the core process remains unchanged.

To further address concerns about generalizability, we would like to note that we have **already instantiating STSBench on the Argoverse2 dataset**. As a first step, we successfully extracted **ego-vehicle scenarios**, which appear **plausible and consistent**, confirming that the framework adapts well to new datasets with minimal changes. While this work began **after submission** and is therefore **beyond the scope of the current paper**, it provides additional evidence that STSBench is **dataset-agnostic and scalable**, supporting broader applicability beyond NuScenes.


**Q1. Plan for future datasets**

Yes, we plan to instantiate STSBench on **Argoverse2**, which offers a broader set of annotated classes (e.g., animals), enabling more diverse and complex scenario definitions. However, we currently do **not plan** to apply it to **Waymo**, as key data modalities are missing from the public release - specifically **rear-view camera images** in the perception dataset and **full sensor coverage** in the motion dataset.

Adapting STSBench to other datasets is **technically straightforward**. The main differences lie in data handling (e.g., formats, coordinate systems), which can be resolved with dataset-specific preprocessing. Moreover, the availability of additional object classes in datasets like Argoverse2 opens the door to defining **new scenario types**, requiring only the addition of corresponding **mining heuristics** - a core design feature of our modular framework.

The **main challenge lies in model evaluation**, not benchmark instantiation. Argoverse2 lacks language annotations, which prevents training or fine-tuning existing driving expert VLMs. Additionally, differences in sensor setups and modalities make **direct model transfer non-trivial**. Thus, while the benchmark extension itself is feasible, evaluating models meaningfully on it remains an open research challenge, one we hope the community will explore as more annotated data becomes available.


**Q2. More fine-grained evaluation metrics**

We agree that introducing more **fine-grained evaluation metrics**, such as **reasoning chain explanations**, would offer a deeper understanding of model behavior and is a promising direction for future work.

As a preliminary step, we conducted experiments prompting **GPT-4o** to explain its answers. Interestingly, the model **reasoned surprisingly insightful**. For instance, in detecting an overtaking maneuver, it described both (1) the relative translation of two vehicles and (2) the transition of the overtaking vehicle across rear, side, and front camera views, demonstrating strong temporal and spatial reasoning. Similarly, in **Figures 20 and 21 of the supplementary material**, the model accurately identified **jaywalking** (without access to map data) and a **left turn**, each supported by plausible reasoning.

We also attempted to elicit reasoning from **driving expert models**, but their responses were often generic or overly aligned with their fine-tuning data, lacking meaningful justification. This is interesting and thus needs further investigation in future research.

We thank the reviewer for the positive and constructive feedback. We appreciate the recognition of STSnu as the **first benchmark explicitly targeting spatio-temporal reasoning in expert VLMs** using multi-view data, as well as their acknowledgement of the benchmark’s **43 diverse scenarios and 971 human-verified questions**, and its ability to **reveal critical limitations in current models' reasoning about complex traffic dynamics**.


**1. Pseudocode for heuristics**

We agree that pseudocode can help illustrate the logical structure of our mining process and will include **one representative pseudocode example for each scenario type** (ego, agent, ego-to-agent, and agent-to-agent) in the **supplementary material**, due to space limitations in the main manuscript.

For full implementation details, we also refer readers to our **open-source code repository**, where all scenario extraction functions are available in *STSBench/annotator/mining/ego.py*.

As a preview, the pseudocode for an *acceleration* maneuver will appear as follows (visualization limited by markdown):

---

**Inputs**
- `objs`: A list of `Ego` or `Agent` objects, each with:
  - `.velocity`: A numeric velocity attribute.
  - `.is_vehicle`: A boolean flag indicating if the object is a vehicle.
- `frames` *(int, optional)*: Number of consecutive frames to evaluate for acceleration (default = 6).
- `threshold_ms` *(float, optional)*: Minimum velocity increase required over the window (default = 3.0).

---

**Outputs**
- A generator yielding `(start_idx, end_idx)` tuples marking intervals of acceleration.
- Returns `(None, None)` if input is invalid or insufficient for analysis.

---

**Steps**

1. If the first object in `objs` is not a vehicle:
    Return `(None, None)`
2. Extract the velocity of each object into a NumPy array `vel`.
3. If the number of velocity samples is less than `frames`:
    Return `(None, None)`
4. Use `np.lib.stride_tricks.sliding_window_view` to create overlapping sequences of `frames` velocities → `vel_w`.
5. Compute first-order velocity differences in each window → `acc_w`.
6. Create a boolean mask where:
   - All differences in `acc_w` are > 0.1 (positive acceleration)
   - Total velocity change in each window (`vel_w[:, -1] - vel_w[:, 0]`) is > `threshold_ms`
7. Apply `merge_true_islands_center(mask)` to smooth valid acceleration regions.
8. For each `start_idx` where `mask` is True:
    Compute `end_idx = start_idx + frames`
    Yield `(start_idx, end_idx)`

---


**2. Sub-sampling details**

We thank the reviewer for the suggestion. We will expand **Section 2.1 of the supplementary material** to include a more detailed description of our sub-sampling strategy, including all thresholds and filtering criteria.

Specifically, we first discard scenarios where the agent is **visible less than 30\% in the first video frame**, using the occlusion rate provided in the NuScenes annotations. Next, we apply **farthest point sampling (FPS)** to ensure an even spatial distribution of agents across the x–y plane. Finally, we remove objects located **beyond 30 meters** from the ego-vehicle, as such distant objects are typically too small or occluded to be meaningfully interpreted by models.


**3. Quantitative comparison related work**

We fully agree that a quantitative comparison would strengthen the Related Work section.

However, this is unfortunately difficult to realize, as **most existing benchmarks do not disclose sufficient details** about their annotation pipelines or verification times. Typically, they release only the final annotations, without detailed documentation of the underlying process, making a fair comparison on metrics like automation level or efficiency infeasible.

That said, we emphasize that STSBench is **transparent by design**: we provide exact statistics on human verification time in the supplementary material, and we openly release both the **scenario mining code** and the **verification tool**, allowing others to reproduce and assess the efficiency of our pipeline.


**4. Statistical measures**

We agree that adding statistical measures improves the interpretability of the results.

To address this, we will include **confidence intervals over five runs** for all models in **Table 2 of the main manuscript**. Due to computational constraints, we have so far been able to run repeated experiments for one representative model from each category, namely **GPT-4o**, **InternVL 2.5 8B**, and **DriveMM**, and report their results below (mean ± std):

| **GPT-4o**          | 58.9 ± 3.0 | 75.2 ± 2.8 | 44.0 ± 2.2 | 43.0 ± 3.4 | 55.3 ± 2.0    |
| **InternVL 2.5 8B** | 38.4 ± 2.4 | 44.6 ± 8.9 | 47.2 ± 1.2 | 43.8 ± 4.7 | 43.5 ± 3.6 |
| **DriveMM**         | 47.8 ± 5.0 | 61.8 ± 11.1 | 38.7 ± 2.3 | 28.0 ± 4.6 | 44.0 ± 2.8 |

We are continuing these experiments for the remaining models and will include all available results in the final version of the paper.


**5. Human verification process analysis**

To complement the raw agreement statistics, we computed **Cohen’s kappa** for all pairs of inspectors (I1, I2, I3) on both mined and negative scenarios. The results (see table below) indicate strong inter-annotator reliability. 


|             |Positive scenarios | Negative scenarios |
| ----------- | ----------------- | ------------------ |
| I1 & I2     | 0.88940           | 0.97333            |
| I1 & I3     | 0.92001           | 0.97822            |
| I2 & I3     | 0.88294           | 0.97767            |


In addition, we calculated **Fleiss’ kappa** to assess overall agreement across all reviewers, which also confirms consistent annotations:

|              |Positive scenarios | Negative scenarios |
| ------------ | ----------------- | ------------------ |
| Fleiss' kappa | 0.87743           | 0.97742            |

To better understand the sources of disagreement, we have already included **qualitative examples with visualizations and explanations** in **Section 2.3 of the supplementary material**, illustrating common cases of ambiguity and how they were resolved.

These additions will be included in the revised version of the paper and supplementary material.


**6. Generalizability of STSBench beyond NuScenes**

We appreciate the reviewer’s concern and clarify that STSBench was designed to be **dataset-agnostic**, even though it is instantiated only on NuScenes in this paper. 

We want to outline this decision based on two significant aspects:

**(1) Instantiation on other datasets:**

We chose to instantiate STSBench solely on NuScenes due to two practical constraints.
First, most existing driving expert VLMs are trained on NuScenes and cannot be directly evaluated on other datasets such as Waymo or Argoverse2, which differ significantly in sensor setups. Second, these alternative datasets currently lack language annotations, making it impossible to train existing driving expert models on them. For this reason, we focused on NuScenes, where both the models and necessary metadata are available.

**(2) Adaptability to different sensor configurations:**

Importantly, our mining framework operates purely on structured annotations, 3D bounding boxes, tracks, class labels, and HD maps, and does not depend on raw sensor data (e.g., images or LiDAR). This makes it **largely independent of sensor configuration**, as long as the dataset provides standard annotations in a common reference frame. Minor adjustments, such as adapting threshold, may be required for different environments (e.g., urban vs. highway), but the core process remains unchanged.

To further address concerns about generalizability, we would like to note that we have **already instantiating STSBench on the Argoverse2 dataset**. As a first step, we successfully extracted **ego-vehicle scenarios**, which appear **plausible and consistent**, confirming that the framework adapts well to new datasets with minimal changes. While this work began **after submission** and is therefore **beyond the scope of the current paper**, it provides additional evidence that STSBench is **dataset-agnostic and scalable**, supporting broader applicability beyond NuScenes.

**7. Future research in conclusion section**

We fully agree with the reviewer and will add a dedicated “**Future Work**” section in the final version of the paper to outline concrete research directions enabled by STSBench.

Future directions include the following:
- **Mining more complex scenarios**, such as multi-agent interactions involving more than two participants or chained events with temporal dependencies.
- **Handling edge cases**, which remains challenging due to limited availability in public datasets, but could be addressed as richer data might become accessible.
- **Finer-grained scenario classification**, potentially incorporating risk assessment metrics based on inter-agent distance, velocity, or occlusion.
- Most importantly, advancing **model design for spatio-temporal reasoning**, either by enhancing current driving expert models with improved training strategies or by developing novel architectures explicitly tailored for multi-view, temporally grounded scene understanding.

These directions reflect both benchmark extensions and the broader vision of driving model advancement that STSBench is intended to support.

We thank the reviewer for the detailed feedback and for recognizing the key contributions of our work, including the introduction of the **first automated pipeline for mining spatio-temporal driving scenarios**, the benchmark’s ability to **expose critical limitations in driving expert VLMs** motivating architectural innovation, and the **clarity and structure of the figures, tables, and overall presentation**.

## 1. Scenario mining
**a, c) Clarification of negative samples**

Negative scenarios are **pre-defined** for each scenario type as part of the scenario catalog. These serve as the initial pool of plausible but incorrect answer choices for the multiple-choice questions. This design ensures that distractors are semantically relevant, i.e., closely related in meaning or behavior, rather than trivially unrelated (e.g., assigning "left turn" as a distractor in a pedestrian-only scenario like "walk alongside"). This approach increases the benchmark's difficulty and better evaluates models’ fine-grained reasoning capabilities.

However, we acknowledge that in real-world scenes, multiple scenarios may co-occur for the same agents. For example, in a "walk alongside" scenario, pedestrians might also be "crossing" or "jaywalking." To address this, we include a **lightweight human verification step after mining**. In this step, inspectors remove any negative scenario that is actually occurring in the scene, i.e., false negatives due to semantic or temporal overlap. 
This refinement is necessary because the automatic mining may either miss these overlaps or introduce false positives. Therefore, we rely on human judgment to ensure that the final set of negatives only includes valid, non-occurring alternatives.

In summary, negative scenarios are **pre-defined but refined during validation** to remove any that unintentionally overlap with the scene’s ground truth. We will clarify this two-step process more explicitly in the final version of the manuscript.

**b) Rules vs. Boundary scenes**

We agree that heuristics inherently depend on fixed thresholds and are limited in capturing the full complexity of real-world dynamics. However, our primary goal is to **construct a high-quality benchmark** that reliably tests the **spatio-temporal reasoning** abilities of driving expert VLMs. To this end, we deliberately focused on well-defined scenarios where spatial and temporal patterns can be extracted with high confidence.

Importantly, even without including boundary scenes, our benchmark already reveals substantial limitations in current driving expert models' reasoning capabilities. The consistent underperformance of models across interaction-heavy scenarios demonstrates the benchmark’s value.

That said, we see extending the framework to include boundary or ambiguous scenes as a natural next step. For example, **relaxing mining thresholds** would allow a broader range of scenes to be included, at the cost of increased manual verification to preserve scenario quality. We consider this a promising direction for future work, especially when model performance saturates on the current benchmark.

**d) Multiple-choice questions**

We agree that template-based generation restricts surface-level variation in question phrasing. However, this design choice was made deliberately to ensure **scalability**, **consistency**, and a clear focus on the intended evaluation target, **spatio-temporal understanding from visual inputs**, rather than language parsing.

In principle, question diversification could be introduced via LLMs or manual rewriting.

However:

**Scalability:** Both approaches would require substantial additional human verification to ensure the correctness and consistency of questions, especially as new scenarios are added over time.

**Isolation of model capabilities:** Uniform question phrasing ensures that performance differences across samples of the same scenario type are not influenced by variation in question wording. This isolates the vision-language model’s reasoning ability rather than its capacity to interpret diverse linguistic styles.

In summary, we intentionally prioritized consistency over diversity to maintain clarity, comparability, and scalability. That said, we acknowledge that future extensions of the benchmark could explore diversified question generation, especially in settings that also test linguistic robustness.

**e) Only static events / 2. c) Binary outcomes**

We agree that continuous decision-making and risk assessment are critical for real-world autonomous driving. 

However, the goal of STSBench is fundamentally different: it evaluates whether models can **correctly identify and understand spatio-temporal scenarios**, such as overtaking, stopping, or crossing, within a fixed time window (3 seconds). The benchmark is not designed to evaluate whether a model should **decide to take an action**, but rather whether it can **correctly recognize that an action is occurring**, based on multi-view visual and temporal context. In this sense, the task emphasizes scenario recognition, not planning or control.

However, we fully agree that incorporating notions of dynamic risk (e.g., “Is this overtaking maneuver dangerous?”) would be a valuable of our work. For instance, scenario-level attributes such as agent speed, distance to other vehicles, or relative acceleration could be incorporated to assess scene difficulty or risk level, further pushing the boundaries of what driving expert VLMs are capable of understanding.

We will mention this direction explicitly as **part of our future work** in the revised manuscript.

**f) Illustration semantic overlap**

As described in **L272–L273 of the main manuscript**, we apply **majority voting for positive scenarios** and retain **only negative scenarios with full agreement** across all inspectors. This conservative approach is designed to minimize ambiguity in answer choices and ensure high annotation quality.

To support transparency, we include a detailed breakdown of the verification process, including rejection reasons, in **Section 2.3 of the supplementary material**. Additionally, **a screenshot of the verification interface** is provided in **Figure 7 of the supplementary material**, illustrating how reviewers inspect and resolve scenario assignments, including ambiguous cases.

## 2. Experiments
**a) Inputs of LLMs and VLMs**

We fully agree that LLMs and VLMs operate under different assumptions and that their inputs are necessarily imbalanced due to their architectural design. In our benchmark, LLMs serve primarily as a **reasoning baseline**: they are tasked with solving the same multiple-choice questions, but without access to visual data. This setup allows us to isolate how much reasoning can be done from structured, symbolic inputs alone (e.g., trajectories), and how that compares to reasoning over raw sensory inputs.

However, LLMs are **not advantageous across the board**. In fact, they operate **without access to map information**, such as crosswalks or lane geometries, which significantly hinders their ability to correctly identify scenarios like “cross,” “jaywalk,” “lane change,” or “left/right turn.” For instance, distinguishing a left turn from a curved trajectory is nearly impossible in the absence of map context, a limitation not shared by VLMs, which can leverage multi-view imagery.

On the other hand, VLMs receive a single image per time step corresponding to the most relevant camera view, along with camera metadata. This can be advantageous in scenarios where spatial progression across views is meaningful (e.g., “agent overtaking ego,” where appearance shifts from rear to side to front view).

We would like to thank the reviewer for the very positive remarks, which highlight in particular the **importance of our benchmark for the autonomous driving community**, the **quality of the presentation**, and its **public availability**.

**1) Limited diversity**

We fully agree that NuScenes has inherent limitations in diversity due to its collection process, which focuses on regular, safe driving behavior. As we noted in the paper’s **limitation section**, this results in a limited variety of annotated object classes and unusual events in the dataset.

Nonetheless, we chose NuScenes for instantiating STSBench because it remains the **most widely used dataset for vision-language driving models**. Many of these models have been trained and fine-tuned on it due to its combination of rich sensor data and publicly available language annotations.

Importantly, **STSBench is not restricted to NuScenes** or its predefined object categories. Our framework is **fully generalizable** and can be applied to any dataset that includes sufficiently detailed ground truth annotations. If a dataset includes labels for objects such as boxes, mats, or other cargo items, STSBench can mine these interactions through new scenario definitions.

For example, to model a "falling object from the vehicle ahead" event, STSBench could identify scenes where an object is initially co-moving with a leading vehicle and subsequently diverges from its path. This can be defined using heuristics based on proximity thresholds and motion trajectories, both of which are already implemented in our framework. Thus, integrating such edge-case scenarios is straightforward once the relevant annotations are available. Specifically, the cargo object must remain within a defined distance of the leading vehicle over time to be considered associated with it.
Once this distance consistently exceeds the threshold, the object can be inferred to have fallen from the vehicle.

We also appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion to integrate STSBench into existing LMM benchmark suites, such as lmms-eval, and will consider this direction for a future code update.

summary.value: This paper addresses the issue that existing benchmarks focus on semantic tasks while neglecting the multi-view spatiotemporal reasoning capabilities. It proposes the STSBench framework, which automatically mines spatiotemporal events in real-world driving scenarios and constructs a high-quality benchmark. A total of 1,188 high-quality scenes are obtained from the NuScenes validation set, resulting in the creation of 971 multiple-choice questions to evaluate the multi-view spatiotemporal reasoning abilities of VLMs in the autonomous driving domain.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. Introduces the first automated pipeline for mining spatio-temporal driving scenarios from existing datasets.
2. Exposes severe limitations in expert VLMs, revealing their inability to model complex interactions and driving architectural innovation.
3. Figures and tables are well-structured and the writting is easy to follow.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
I have some concerns about the dataset construction process and experiments:
1. About the scenario mining
    + The paper claims to pre-define negative scenarios before mining, yet human verification removes invalid negatives post-mining. ​Authors must clarify whether negative scenarios are pre-defined or dynamically adjusted.​​
    + The scene definition relies on manually designed rules, which will cause it to fail in boundary scenes. 
    + Negative sample design does not consider semantic overlap.
    + Generating multiple-choice questions based on rule templates will result in poor question diversity.
    + The questions only test static events (e.g., “whether to overtake”) and do not assess continuous decision-making, where overtaking may be dangerous.
    + ​Figure 2 ‘s bottom-left "Verification" module fails to illustrate how inspectors reconcile semantic overlaps. A demo of the actual verification interface should be added to demonstrate how ambiguous cases are resolved.
2. About the experiments
    + The inputs of LLM and VLM in Table 2 are different. The advantage of LLMs may come from the input advantage rather than the reasoning ability, which needs to be discussed. Ablation experiments (e.g. on VLMs input trajectories) should be added to verify this bias. 
    + It seems that the only evaluation metric is accuracy, and there is a lack of specific analysis of why LLM/VLM performs poorly. A confusion matrix or case visualization should be provided instead of simply stating that the model is not powerful enough.
    + The benchmark tests binary outcomes but ignores continuous decision-making. This misaligns with real driving needs where risk evolves over time.
    + The paper emphasizes that STSBench can be extended to any dataset, but it is only instantiated on NuScenes. The framework has not been tested on other datasets (such as Waymo or Argoverse), and its adaptability to different sensor configurations cannot be demonstrated.

summary.value: The authors proposed STSBench, an automated framework for mining spatio-temporal driving scenarios from existing datasets with rich ground-truth annotations, which can automatically extract traffic scenarios, provide an intuitive interface for human verification, and generate multiple-choice questions for evaluating vision-language models' holistic understanding in autonomous driving.

strengths_contributions.value: The authors instantiated STSBench on the NuScenes dataset to create STSnu, the first benchmark specifically targeting spatio-temporal reasoning capabilities of driving expert VLMs across multi-view cameras, comprising 43 diverse scenarios and 971 human-verified questions that reveal critical limitations in existing models' ability to reason about complex traffic dynamics.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. In the Scenario Definition section, given the logically rigorous nature of heuristic algorithms, incorporating pseudocode in the corresponding section would help better demonstrate their implementation workflow.
2. In Section 3.3, the sub-sampling strategy based on "occlusion rate and spatial distribution" needs more detailed explanation with specific thresholds and criteria used for filtering scenarios.
3. In the Related Work section, a quantitative comparison table showing how STSBench differs from existing benchmarks in terms of automation level, scenario coverage, and verification efficiency would strengthen the contribution.
4. In the Experiments section, statistical significance tests and confidence intervals for the accuracy results should be provided to validate the performance differences between model categories.
5. In the human verification process, the inter-annotator agreement statistics (85.6% for positive, 20.8% disagreement for negative) should be analyzed more thoroughly with Cohen's kappa or similar metrics.
6. The generalizability of STSBench to other datasets beyond NuScenes should be experimentally validated by applying the framework to at least one additional dataset like Waymo or ArgoVerse.
7. In the Conclusion section, specific future research directions should be discussed, such as incorporating more complex scenarios, handling edge cases, or developing models specifically designed for spatio-temporal reasoning in multi-view settings.

summary.value: This paper proposes STSBench, a benchmarking framework for evaluating the spatio-temporal reasoning capabilities of multi-modal large language models in autonomous driving. The authors combine automated mining with manual verification to efficiently extract various complex traffic scenarios from datasets such as NuScenes, and automatically generate multiple-choice questions for evaluation. The authors conduct systematic evaluations of mainstream LLMs, general-purpose VLMs, and expert VLMs, revealing current models’ shortcomings in complex spatio-temporal reasoning.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. The proposed annotation framework can create benchmarks for any given perception dataset,  greatly improving the efficiency of benchmark construction.
2. The benchmark covers multi-modal, multi-view, and multi-frame data. The questions are systematically designed with a reasonable difficulty distribution, truly reflecting models’ spatio-temporal reasoning abilities.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. The number of models evaluated on the benchmark is relatively small.
2. Due to the limitations of public datasets, extreme and dangerous scenarios are underrepresented, which may affect the challenge and representativeness of the benchmark.
3. The benchmark is mainly based on the NuScenes dataset and has not yet been validated for generalizability on more diverse datasets.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

additional_feedback.value:
Questions for the Authors:

1. The STSBench framework is currently instantiated mainly on the NuScenes validation set. Do the authors plan to apply it to other public datasets such as Waymo or Argoverse? What are the main challenges encountered when adapting to different datasets?
2. Currently, STSnu mainly uses multiple-choice accuracy to evaluate models. Do the authors consider introducing more fine-grained evaluation metrics (such as reasoning chain explanations) to more comprehensively assess the decision-making process of models?

Suggestions for Improvement:

It is suggested to test more VLMs and LLMs, for example, by evaluating models with relatively larger parameter sizes.

title.value: STSBench: A Spatio-temporal Scenario Benchmark for Multi-modal Large Language Models in Autonomous Driving

TLDR.value: STSBench is a benchmark that evaluates the capabilities of Multi-modal Large Language Models to reason about spatio-temporal actions.

abstract.value: We introduce STSBench, a scenario-based framework to benchmark the holistic understanding of vision-language models (VLMs) for autonomous driving. The framework automatically mines predefined traffic scenarios from any dataset using ground-truth annotations, provides an intuitive user interface for efficient human verification, and generates multiple-choice questions for model evaluation. Applied to the nuScenes dataset, we present STSnu, the first benchmark that evaluates the spatio-temporal reasoning capabilities of VLMs based on comprehensive 3D perception. Existing benchmarks typically target off-the-shelf or fine-tuned VLMs for images or videos from a single viewpoint, focusing on semantic tasks such as object recognition, dense captioning, risk assessment, or scene understanding. In contrast, STSnu evaluates driving expert VLMs for end-to-end driving, operating on videos from multi-view cameras or LiDAR. It specifically assesses their ability to reason about both ego-vehicle actions and complex interactions among traffic participants, a crucial capability for autonomous vehicles. The benchmark features 43 diverse scenarios spanning multiple views and frames, resulting in 971 human-verified multiple-choice questions. A thorough evaluation uncovers critical shortcomings in existing models’ ability to reason about fundamental traffic dynamics in complex environments. These findings highlight the urgent need for architectural advancements that explicitly model spatio-temporal reasoning. By addressing a core gap in spatio-temporal evaluation, STSBench enables the development of more robust and explainable VLMs for autonomous driving.
